\section{Introduction}

Evaluating the safety of open-weight language models currently requires generating text, judging each output for harmful content, and aggregating scores across hundreds of prompts \cite{Mazeika2024, Rottger2023}. This pipeline is slow, sensitive to prompt phrasing, and must be re-run whenever a model is modified. The proliferation of post-hoc modifications to released checkpoints---quantisation, adapter merging, and abliteration \cite{Arditi2024}---makes repeated evaluation expensive and raises the question of whether safety-relevant information can be read directly from a model's activations.

Recent work has shown that such information is linearly decodable from mid-layer activations. The Activation-based Model Scanner (AMS) extracts a concept direction from 16 contrastive prompt pairs and predicts behavioural compliance across 14 checkpoints \cite{Messenger2026}. N-GLARE computes Jensen--Shannon divergence across layer groups and reports coupling with refusal rates during training \cite{Lin2025}. Representation engineering uses contrastive activations for monitoring and control across safety-relevant attributes \cite{Zou2023}. All three systems read activations at the final prompt token.

A readout that is to replace a behavioural benchmark must satisfy two properties beyond correlation with harmful compliance. First, it must be \emph{specific}: it should not fire on checkpoint modifications that do not change safety behaviour. A dtype cast, a re-download of the same weights, or a non-safety fine-tune should not trigger an alarm. Second, it must be \emph{two-sided}: it should capture over-refusal---the tendency to refuse benign requests---and not only compliance with harmful ones, because a blanket refuser scores perfectly on compliance yet fails as a deployed model. Neither property has been tested for any activation-based safety readout. AMS reports quantisation drift of at most 4.4\% on a single model but does not grade whether the quantised model's behaviour actually changed \cite{Messenger2026}. No system uses over-refusal as a target for an internal readout.

A separate question is whether the relationship between internal representations and behaviour is \emph{causal}. The refusal direction identified by Arditi et al.\ is linearly decodable from prompt-site activations across 13 chat models \cite{Arditi2024}, but decodability does not imply that removing the direction at a specific site changes behaviour. Galeone et al.\ showed that detection accuracy and steerability are dissociated \cite{Galeone2026}. Orgad et al.\ demonstrated that harmful-response generation and harm recognition use distinct mechanisms \cite{Orgad2026}. These findings raise the possibility that a direction may be present in activations---readable by a probe---without being \emph{used} by downstream computation at that site.

We address both questions---specificity and causality---with two experiments on the same set of models and directions.

[FIGURE:fig_overview]

\paragraph{Summary of Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Activation readouts have far fewer false alarms than the logit baseline.} On 15 behavioural no-ops (dtype casts, re-downloads, system-prompt swaps, non-safety LoRA and DPO) across three model families, the request-axis Cohen's $d$ fires on 1/15 pairs (93\% specificity) and the benign-side separability score fires on 0/15 (100\%). The final-layer logit gap fires on 6/15 (60\%) and the weight-space cosine on 9/15 (40\%). This is the first per-checkpoint false-alarm audit of activation-based safety readouts on behaviourally graded no-ops (Section~\ref{sec:results-specificity}).

\item \textbf{The refusal direction is decodable but causally inert at the prompt site.} In a 6-band $\times$ 3-site causal intervention grid on Qwen3-4B, removing the fitted refusal direction at the last prompt token changes the first generated token---keyword-proxy refusal drops from 0.79 to 0.15---but does not change judged refusal in any of 18 cells for either instruct or SafeRL models. The model rewrites its refusal in different words. This ``decodable but inert'' pattern holds in 12/12 instruct cells and 12/12 SafeRL cells at the prompt site (Section~\ref{sec:results-causal}).

\item \textbf{Over-refusal, not harmful compliance, is the causal lever.} The only cell that survives Holm correction across the 18-cell grid is the benign-side direction N6 at the last prompt token in the middle depth band (B5), which reduces over-refusal in the instruct model. SafeRL is more robust: global removal of the refusal direction at the same band drops instruct refusal to 0.67 while SafeRL shows a difference-in-differences of $+0.23$ (Section~\ref{sec:results-causal}).

\item \textbf{AMS Tier-2 detects zero effective changes.} The reference-based AMS verify rule fires on 0/8 effective parent--child pairs, including five community-abliterated checkpoints. AMS Tier-1 $\sigma$ has perfect specificity (0/15 false alarms) but detects only 3/8 effective changes (Section~\ref{sec:results-specificity}).
\end{enumerate}


\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Activation-based safety readouts.}
AMS extracts concept directions from contrastive prompt pairs at 40--80\% depth and reports leave-one-out threshold accuracy of 71\% across 14 configurations from four families \cite{Messenger2026}. N-GLARE aggregates Jensen--Shannon divergence of hidden states and reports coupling with training-time refusal rates \cite{Lin2025}. RAS uses a reference-anchored score calibrated within families \cite{Huang2026}. Aligned Probing correlates per-layer probe accuracy with output toxicity and shows stability under quantisation for OLMo \cite{Waldis2025}. All four read activations at the final prompt token. AMS identifies decode-time analysis as its principal open problem \cite{Messenger2026}.

\paragraph{False-alarm and staleness controls.}
AMS reports FP16/INT8/INT4 drift of at most 4.4\% on a single model outside its validated panel but does not grade whether the quantised model's behaviour changed \cite{Messenger2026}. Duan benchmarks frozen linear probes across quantisation, LoRA and QLoRA conditions and finds that fine-tuning-style updates make probes stale, with big-drop rates of 43--54\% \cite{Duan2026}. Hurtado audits 37 benign fine-tunes and merges at FPR 0.11 using a reference-anchored weight-space signal \cite{Hurtado2026}. No prior work grades the behaviour of each variant before calling it a no-op.

\paragraph{Decodability versus causality.}
Arditi et al.\ showed that a single direction mediates refusal across 13 models \cite{Arditi2024}. Galeone et al.\ found that detection accuracy and steerability are dissociated: models whose harm representations are perfectly decodable are not necessarily steerable along those directions \cite{Galeone2026}. Bosco and Srinivasan used orthogonalised-random controls and showed that removing the mapped direction raises attack success far above the random baseline \cite{Bosco2026}. Yang et al.\ showed that the refusal signal of reasoning models drops at the first generated token \cite{Yang2026}. Mitra demonstrated that prompt-time defences are blind to prefilling attacks and that the first generated token carries distinct safety information \cite{Mitra2026}.

\paragraph{Over-refusal.}
XSTest provides paired harmful and benign prompts to measure exaggerated safety behaviours \cite{Rottger2023}. Jiang et al.\ measure per-model over-refusal as a behavioural audit outcome and show that static probes fail to distinguish jailbroken from base models \cite{Jiang2026}. Every existing over-refusal measurement is a behavioural outcome; no internal readout has been scored against over-refusal as its target.


\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{Experiment 1: Specificity Audit}
\label{sec:exp1-method}

\paragraph{Models and families.}
We construct parent--child pairs across three model families: Qwen3 (Qwen3-0.6B-Instruct, F1), Llama-3.2 (Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, F2) and Falcon3 (Falcon3-1B-Instruct, F3). Each parent is modified with seven expression-only changes intended as behavioural no-ops: (1) a trivial re-save round-trip, (2) bf16-to-fp16 cast, (3) int8 weight-only quantisation, (4) system-prompt swap, (5) LLM.int8() quantisation \cite{Dettmers2022}, (6) a short non-safety LoRA on Dolly instructions \cite{Hu2021}, and (7) a short non-safety DPO step on Dolly-derived coherence pairs \cite{Rafailov2023}. Additionally, we include nine effective changes: in-house rank-one directional lesions at $\alpha \in \{0.5, 1.0\}$ \cite{Arditi2024} per family and community-abliterated children from Hugging Face (five abliterated checkpoints plus AMD-OLMo base-to-SFT).

\paragraph{Behavioural grading.}
Each checkpoint is evaluated on 85 harmful prompts (from XSTest \cite{Rottger2023} and JailbreakBench \cite{Mazeika2024}) and 83 paired benign twins with greedy decoding at 96 new tokens. Harmful compliance (HC) is the fraction of harmful prompts answered substantively; over-refusal (OR) is the fraction of benign prompts incorrectly refused. Both are judged by a separate LLM grader. A pair is classified as NOOP if $|\Delta\text{HC}| \leq 0.05$ and $|\Delta\text{OR}| \leq 0.05$ with both 95\% paired-bootstrap CIs inside $[-0.10, +0.10]$; as EFFECTIVE if the $\Delta$HC CI excludes zero; as OR\_EFFECTIVE if the $\Delta$OR CI excludes zero but $\Delta$HC covers zero. Behavioural grading is committed before any activation readout is computed, enforced by a SHA-256 hash chain.

\paragraph{Readouts.}
For each parent and child, we extract residual-stream activations at the last prompt token at every layer. We compute:
\begin{itemize}
\item $N1$ (request-axis $d$): Cohen's $d$ on EASY-fit/HARD-score prompts at the layer maximising separation.
\item $N6$ (benign-side separability): Cohen's $d$ between XSTest safe twins and matched harmful prompts, measuring the benign direction.
\item $C7$: cross-layer cosine alignment of the per-layer diff-in-means directions.
\item BL1 (logit baseline): final-layer logit gap between the top refusal token and the top compliance token, in three variants (BL1\_easy, BL1\_hard, BL1\_truelogit).
\item AMS Tier-1 $\sigma$: faithfully reimplemented from the released Apache-2.0 code \cite{Messenger2026}, using the 16 \texttt{harmful\_content} pairs at 40--80\% depth.
\item AMS Tier-2 drift: the reference-based verify rule (direction cosine $\geq 0.8$ and relative separation drift $\leq 0.2$).
\item $B7$: weight-space cosine between the parent's and child's per-layer diff-in-means weight projections, with architecture-mandated null directions projected out.
\end{itemize}
For each readout, we compute the paired change $\Delta$ (child minus parent) with a 1000-draw prompt-stratified bootstrap CI. A readout fires a false alarm on a no-op pair if its $\Delta$ CI excludes zero.

\subsection{Experiment 2: Causal Intervention Grid}
\label{sec:exp2-method}

\paragraph{Models.}
We use three Qwen3-4B variants: Instruct, SafeRL (additional safety reinforcement learning) and an abliterated checkpoint (mlabonne/Qwen3-4B-abliterated).

\paragraph{Grid design.}
We cross six depth bands (B1--B6, each spanning one-sixth of the 36-layer stack) with three sites: P (last prompt token), D$'$ (model's own first 1--8 greedy decode positions, teacher-forced) and E (early response window, positions 5--20). Each cell has four arms:
\begin{itemize}
\item Arm F: matched-norm projection removing the fitted request-axis direction.
\item Arm N6: matched-norm projection removing the benign-side direction.
\item Arm R: an orthogonalised random direction with matched norm, averaged over 10--20 draws.
\item Arm 0: no intervention (baseline).
\end{itemize}
An additional positive-control arm (full-residual patching) runs on a two-cell subset.

\paragraph{Outcomes.}
For each cell and arm, we generate 80 new tokens on 48 harmful prompts and 48 benign-borderline prompts and judge refusal, over-refusal and compliance using the same LLM grader as Experiment~1. A cell is \emph{causal} only if the F (or N6) arm differs from the R arm (not merely from arm 0), to rule out generic disruption. All 18 cells per model are tested jointly with Holm--Bonferroni correction at $\alpha = 0.05$.

\paragraph{Decodable-but-inert classification.}
A cell is classified as ``decodable but inert'' if (a) the direction is linearly decodable from arm-0 activations (AUROC $> 0.70$) and (b) the arm-F (or arm-N6) versus arm-R contrast does not reach significance.


\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Specificity: False Alarms on Behavioural No-Ops}
\label{sec:results-specificity}

Table~\ref{tab:specificity} reports the false-alarm rate (fraction of no-op pairs where the readout's $\Delta$ CI excludes zero) and sensitivity (fraction of effective pairs detected) for each readout class.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{False-alarm rate and sensitivity on 15 behavioural no-ops and 9 effective changes across three families. Activation readouts fire on 0--1 no-ops; logit and weight-space readouts fire on 6--9.}
\label{tab:specificity}
\begin{tabular}{lccl}
\toprule
\textbf{Readout} & \textbf{FA (of 15)} & \textbf{Sens.\ (of 9)} & \textbf{False-alarm pairs} \\
\midrule
N6 (benign sep.)       & 0/15 & 5/9 & --- \\
N4 (shape/onset)       & 0/15 & 3/9 & --- \\
N8 (severity $\rho$)   & 0/15 & 4/8 & --- \\
N9 (decode tok-1)      & 0/15 & 4/8 & --- \\
AMS $\sigma$ (Tier-1)  & 0/15 & 3/8 & --- \\
N1 (request-axis $d$)  & 1/15 & 5/9 & F3\_dpo \\
C7 (cross-layer cos)   & 1/15 & 6/9 & F3\_dpo \\
\midrule
BL1\_easy              & 6/15 & 5/9 & int8wo$\times$2, sysprompt, wu05$\times$2, int8bnb \\
BL1\_truelogit         & 8/15 & 6/9 & +fp16, a05, dpo \\
B7 (weight cosine)     & 9/15 & 7/9 & int8wo$\times$3, fp16$\times$3, int8bnb$\times$2, a05 \\
AMS Tier-2 (drift)     & 0/15 & 0/8 & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The activation readouts (N1, N6, N4, N8, N9, C7, AMS $\sigma$) fire on at most 1 of 15 no-ops (Wilson 95\% CI for 1/15: [0.01, 0.30]). The logit baseline BL1\_easy fires on 6/15 (40\%; Wilson CI [0.20, 0.64]): int8 weight-only quantisation, system-prompt swaps and head-only unembedding edits all shift the final-layer logit gap without changing judged behaviour. The weight-space cosine B7 is worse still, firing on 9/15 (60\%). Every dtype cast (fp16, int8wo, int8bnb) moves B7 because the weight matrices change numerically even though behaviour does not.

Among the baselines, AMS Tier-2 achieves perfect specificity (0/15) but detects zero effective changes (0/8), including five community-abliterated checkpoints. The reference-based verify rule requires the child's direction cosine to exceed 0.8 and its drift to stay below 0.2; abliterated checkpoints violate the cosine threshold but are not flagged because AMS Tier-2 is a \emph{pass/fail} gate, not a \emph{change} detector.

\paragraph{Sensitivity.}
The activation readouts detect 3--6 of 9 effective changes. The logit baselines detect 5--6. Neither class reaches the sensitivity of the weight-space cosine (7/9), but B7's sensitivity comes at the cost of a 60\% false-alarm rate. The trade-off is clear: activation readouts sacrifice some sensitivity for dramatically better specificity.

[FIGURE:fig_specificity]


\subsection{Causal Grid: Decodable but Inert}
\label{sec:results-causal}

\paragraph{No site-local intervention changes judged refusal.}
Across the 18-cell grid (6 bands $\times$ 3 sites), removing the refusal direction F at a single site produces zero causal cells for judged refusal on harmful prompts, in both the instruct and SafeRL models (Table~\ref{tab:causal_headline}). The same holds for the benign-side direction N6 on harmful compliance, and for the positive control.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Causal cells surviving Holm correction ($\alpha = 0.05$) across the 18-cell grid. Refusal on harmful prompts: 0/18 for all arms in all models. Over-refusal on benign-borderline prompts: 1/18 (instruct N6 at P, band B5).}
\label{tab:causal_headline}
\begin{tabular}{llcccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Outcome} & \textbf{F} & \textbf{N6} & \textbf{N6$\perp$} & \textbf{POS} \\
\midrule
Instruct    & Refused (harm)    & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
Instruct    & Over-refusal (hb) & 0 & \textbf{1} & 0 & 0 \\
SafeRL      & Refused (harm)    & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
SafeRL      & Over-refusal (hb) & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
Abliterated & Refused (harm)    & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
Abliterated & Over-refusal (hb) & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Token-1 moves but judged refusal does not.}
Removing F at the prompt site in bands B4--B6 shifts the first-token refusal-onset log-mass by $-2.9$ nats in the instruct model. A keyword-based refusal proxy drops from 0.79 to 0.15, which would appear as a successful jailbreak under keyword-matching evaluation. However, the LLM-judged refusal rate does not change: the model replaces its canonical refusal phrasing (e.g., ``I'm unable to help with that'') with alternative formulations (e.g., ``Creating malware is illegal and I cannot assist''). SafeRL uses ``It's important to clarify'' as its refusal template, which the keyword proxy does not recognise at all ($\kappa = 0$ between keyword and judge labels for SafeRL).

\paragraph{Decodable but inert.}
Table~\ref{tab:decodable_inert} reports the count of cells classified as decodable but inert: the direction is linearly decodable from arm-0 activations but removing it does not change judged behaviour.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Decodable-but-inert cells. The refusal direction F is decodable at the prompt site in every cell where the model refuses, yet removing it never changes judged refusal.}
\label{tab:decodable_inert}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{F on refused\_harm} & \textbf{N6 on over-refusal} \\
\midrule
Instruct    & 12/12 & 11/12 \\
SafeRL      & 12/12 & 12/12 \\
Abliterated &  6/6  &  6/6  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Over-refusal is the causal lever.}
The single cell that survives Holm correction is N6 at site P, band B5, for over-refusal on benign-borderline prompts in the instruct model. Over-refusal drops by 0.12--0.19 at bands B4--B5 before correction. SafeRL shows no causal over-refusal cells: global removal of F at band B4 drops instruct refusal to 0.67, but SafeRL's difference-in-differences is $+0.23$, consistent with its additional safety reinforcement learning providing deeper redundancy.

\paragraph{Abliterated checkpoint.}
The abliterated model's refusal direction has cosine similarity $\sim$0.3 with the instruct direction from band B4 onward, compared to $\sim$0.9 at bands B1--B3. Removing the abliterated model's own fitted F direction at the prompt site \emph{raises} refusal-onset log-mass, the opposite of the instruct pattern. The abliteration procedure rotates the representation rather than erasing it, consistent with Galeone et al.'s finding that detection and control are dissociated \cite{Galeone2026}.

[FIGURE:fig_causal_grid]


\subsection{Commissioned Qwen3-4B Comparison}
\label{sec:results-qwen}

\midrule

Two patterns emerge. First, BL1 ranks SafeRL below Instruct (3.07 vs 4.99) despite SafeRL having zero harmful compliance and zero over-refusal, while Instruct has 11\% over-refusal. N1 and AMS $\sigma$ rank SafeRL and Instruct comparably (2.34 vs 2.45; 6.41 vs 5.73). Second, the abliterated checkpoint's N6 (benign-side separability, 1.79) barely drops from Instruct's value (1.87), while N1 drops sharply (0.71 vs 2.45). The model retains the representation that distinguishes safe from borderline content even after the execution-side refusal direction is removed, consistent with the recognition-execution dissociation reported by Orgad et al.\ \cite{Orgad2026}.


\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\subsection{Why Logit Baselines Fail the Specificity Test}

The final-layer logit gap measures the difference between the probability of the top refusal token and the top compliance token at the last prompt position. Any perturbation that shifts these probabilities---even by a small amount that does not change the greedy decode---produces a nonzero $\Delta$BL1. Quantisation and dtype casts change the numerical precision of the logit computation, system-prompt swaps change the input distribution, and head-only unembedding edits change the projection matrix. All of these move BL1 without moving behaviour because BL1 operates at the decision boundary while behaviour depends on the argmax.

Activation readouts, by contrast, measure the geometry of the representation space at mid-depth layers, which is more stable under these perturbations. The diff-in-means direction at layer 14 of Qwen3-0.6B is bitwise identical between the bf16 reference and the fp16 cast (the activations are computed in bf16 regardless of storage precision), and the int8 weight-only round-trip changes activations by less than $10^{-3}$ in norm.

\subsection{Decodable but Inert: Implications for Safety Monitoring}

The finding that the refusal direction is decodable at the prompt site but removing it does not change judged refusal has two implications. First, keyword-based refusal detection is unreliable. The keyword proxy reports a 64-percentage-point drop in refusal under site-local F removal, but this reflects a change in phrasing, not in policy. An evaluation that counts ``I cannot'' as refusal and ``This is illegal and I cannot assist'' as compliance will overestimate the effectiveness of interventions. Second, the model's refusal policy is implemented redundantly. Even after the dominant linear direction is removed at one site, the model recovers its refusal through alternative representations or later layers. Global removal of F at all positions and all layers does reduce judged refusal (instruct drops to 0.67), confirming that the direction carries causal information in aggregate, but no single site is sufficient.

This finding extends Galeone et al.'s detection-control dissociation \cite{Galeone2026} from the cross-model setting (where different models show different steerability) to the within-model setting (where different sites within the same model show different causal strength).

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\textbf{Scale.} The specificity audit uses three families at 0.6--1.7B parameters. Larger models may have different false-alarm profiles, and the 15 no-ops, while spanning a range of deployment-relevant modifications, do not cover every possible perturbation.

\textbf{Sensitivity gap.} The activation readouts detect 3--6 of 9 effective changes compared to 5--6 for BL1. Whether this gap closes at larger panel sizes is an open question that the pre-registered confirmation panel (at least 30 new checkpoints from at least 8 new families) is designed to answer.

\textbf{Single architecture for the causal grid.} The causal experiment uses only Qwen3-4B variants. The decodable-but-inert finding may not hold for architectures with different attention patterns or layer counts.

\textbf{Judge limitations.} All behavioural outcomes depend on an LLM judge. The judge achieves high agreement with human labels on a calibration set, but systematic biases (e.g., toward labelling longer responses as compliant) cannot be ruled out.

\textbf{No surviving candidate.} No readout passes the full pre-registered selection rule, because the required gap of 1.0 null-SD below BL1's median no-op displacement is unattainable: the activation readouts' median displacement is already near zero, and BL1's is only moderately above zero. The pre-registered bar was set before the magnitude of BL1's false-alarm rate was known.


\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We audited activation-based safety readouts for two properties that a replacement for behavioural benchmarks must have: specificity (no false alarms on no-ops) and causal relevance (the direction matters for behaviour, not just for a probe). Activation readouts at mid-layer depth pass the specificity test with at most 1/15 false alarms, while the final-layer logit gap fails it with 6--8/15. The causal grid reveals that the refusal direction is decodable at every prompt-site cell but removing it changes the first token without changing judged refusal---a dissociation between the keyword proxy and actual safety behaviour that calls for judge-based evaluation in future intervention studies. The single causal lever is over-refusal under the benign-side direction, and SafeRL provides deeper redundancy than standard instruction tuning. These findings establish the false-alarm audit as a necessary validation step for any activation-based safety metric and identify the decodable-but-inert phenomenon as a constraint on site-local causal claims.

\bibliography{references}
\bibliographystyle{plainnat}

An evaluation that counts ``I cannot'' as refusal and ``This is illegal and I cannot assist'' as compliance will overestimate the effectiveness of interventions. Second, the model's refusal policy is implemented redundantly. Even after the dominant linear direction is removed at one site, the model recovers its refusal through alternative representations or later layers. Global removal of F at all positions and all layers does reduce judged refusal (instruct drops to 0.67), confirming that the direction carries causal information in aggregate, but no single site is sufficient.\n\nThis finding extends Galeone et al.'s detection-control dissociation \\cite{Galeone2026} from the cross-model setting (where different models show different steerability) to the within-model setting (where different sites within the same model show different causal strength).\n\n\\subsection{Limitations}\n\\label{sec:limitations}\n\n\\textbf{Scale.} The specificity audit uses three families at 0.6--1.7B parameters. Larger models may have different false-alarm profiles, and the 15 no-ops, while spanning a range of deployment-relevant modifications, do not cover every possible perturbation.\n\n\\textbf{Sensitivity gap.} The activation readouts detect 3--6 of 9 effective changes compared to 5--6 for BL1. Whether this gap closes at larger panel sizes is an open question that the pre-registered confirmation panel (at least 30 new checkpoints from at least 8 new families) is designed to answer.\n\n\\textbf{Single architecture for the causal grid.} The causal experiment uses only Qwen3-4B variants. The decodable-but-inert finding may not hold for architectures with different attention patterns or layer counts.\n\n\\textbf{Judge limitations.} All behavioural outcomes depend on an LLM judge. The judge achieves high agreement with human labels on a calibration set, but systematic biases (e.g., toward labelling longer responses as compliant) cannot be ruled out.\n\n\\textbf{No surviving candidate.} No readout passes the full pre-registered selection rule, because the required gap of 1.0 null-SD below BL1's median no-op displacement is unattainable: the activation readouts' median displacement is already near zero, and BL1's is only moderately above zero. The pre-registered bar was set before the magnitude of BL1's false-alarm rate was known.\n\n\n\\section{Conclusion}\n\\label{sec:conclusion}\n\nWe audited activation-based safety readouts for two properties that a replacement for behavioural benchmarks must have: specificity (no false alarms on no-ops) and causal relevance (the direction matters for behaviour, not just for a probe). Activation readouts at mid-layer depth pass the specificity test with at most 1/15 false alarms, while the final-layer logit gap fails it with 6--8/15. The causal grid reveals that the refusal direction is decodable at every prompt-site cell but removing it changes the first token without changing judged refusal---a dissociation between the keyword proxy and actual safety behaviour that calls for judge-based evaluation in future intervention studies. The single causal lever is over-refusal under the benign-side direction, and SafeRL provides deeper redundancy than standard instruction tuning. These findings establish the false-alarm audit as a necessary validation step for any activation-based safety metric and identify the decodable-but-inert phenomenon as a constraint on site-local causal claims.\n\n\\bibliography{references}\n\\bibliographystyle{plainnat}\n", "structuredPatch": [], "originalFile": null, "userModified": false}

Any perturbation that shifts these probabilities---even by a small amount that does not change the greedy decode---produces a nonzero $\\Delta$BL1. Larger models may have different false-alarm profiles, and the 15 no-ops, while spanning a range of deployment-relevant modifications, do not cover every possible perturbation.\n\n\\textbf{Sensitivity gap.} The activation readouts detect 3--6 of 9 effective changes compared to 5--6 for BL1. Whether this gap closes at larger panel sizes is an open question that the pre-registered confirmation panel (at least 30 new checkpoints from at least 8 new families) is designed to answer.\n\n\\textbf{Single architecture for the causal grid.} The causal experiment uses only Qwen3-4B variants. The decodable-but-inert finding may not hold for architectures with different attention patterns or layer counts.\n\n\\textbf{Judge limitations.} All behavioural outcomes depend on an LLM judge. Activation-based safety readouts promise to replace slow behavioural benchmarks for evaluating open-weight language models, but two validation questions remain open: do these readouts avoid false alarms on checkpoint modifications that do not change safety behaviour, and does the information they read causally influence the model's output? We construct 15 behavioural no-ops (dtype casts, re-downloads, non-safety fine-tunes) and 9 effective changes across three model families and audit seven activation readouts, the final-layer logit gap and weight-space baselines. These results establish false-alarm auditing as a necessary validation step for activation-based safety metrics and identify a decodable-but-inert regime in which strong linear readability does not imply site-local causal control.

Jiang et al.\\ measure per-model over-refusal as a behavioural audit outcome and show that static probes fail to distinguish jailbroken from base models \\cite{Jiang2026}. Every existing over-refusal measurement is a behavioural outcome; no internal readout has been scored against over-refusal as its target.\n\n\n\\section{Method}\n\\label{sec:method}\n\n\\subsection{Experiment 1: Specificity Audit}\n\\label{sec:exp1-method}\n\n\\paragraph{Models and families.}\nWe construct parent--child pairs across three model families: Qwen3 (Qwen3-0.6B-Instruct, F1), Llama-3.2 (Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, F2) and Falcon3 (Falcon3-1B-Instruct, F3). Each parent is modified with seven expression-only changes intended as behavioural no-ops: (1) a trivial re-save round-trip, (2) bf16-to-fp16 cast, (3) int8 weight-only quantisation, (4) system-prompt swap, (5) LLM.int8() quantisation \\cite{Dettmers2022}, (6) a short non-safety LoRA on Dolly instructions \\cite{Hu2021}, and (7) a short non-safety DPO step on Dolly-derived coherence pairs \\cite{Rafailov2023}. Additionally, we include nine effective changes: in-house rank-one directional lesions at $\\alpha \\in \\{0.5, 1.0\\}$ \\cite{Arditi2024} per family and community-abliterated children from Hugging Face (five abliterated checkpoints plus AMD-OLMo base-to-SFT).\n\n\\paragraph{Behavioural grading.}\nEach checkpoint is evaluated on 85 harmful prompts (from XSTest \\cite{Rottger2023} and JailbreakBench \\cite{Mazeika2024}) and 83 paired benign twins with greedy decoding at 96 new tokens. Harmful compliance (HC) is the fraction of harmful prompts answered substantively; over-refusal (OR) is the fraction of benign prompts incorrectly refused. Both are judged by a separate LLM grader. A pair is classified as NOOP if $|\\Delta\\text{HC}| \\leq 0.05$ and $|\\Delta\\text{OR}| \\leq 0.05$ with both 95\\% paired-bootstrap CIs inside $[-0.10, +0.10]$; as EFFECTIVE if the $\\Delta$HC CI excludes zero; as OR\\_EFFECTIVE if the $\\Delta$OR CI excludes zero but $\\Delta$HC covers zero. Behavioural grading is committed before any activation readout is computed, enforced by a SHA-256 hash chain.\n\n\\paragraph{Readouts.}\nFor each parent and child, we extract residual-stream activations at the last prompt token at every layer. We compute:\n\\begin{itemize}\n\\item $N1$ (request-axis $d$): Cohen's $d$ on EASY-fit/HARD-score prompts at the layer maximising separation.\n\\item $N6$ (benign-side separability): Cohen's $d$ between XSTest safe twins and matched harmful prompts, measuring the benign direction.\n\\item $C7$: cross-layer cosine alignment of the per-layer diff-in-means directions.\n\\item BL1 (logit baseline): final-layer logit gap between the top refusal token and the top compliance token, in three variants (BL1\\_easy, BL1\\_hard, BL1\\_truelogit).\n\\item AMS Tier-1 $\\sigma$: faithfully reimplemented from the released Apache-2.0 code \\cite{Messenger2026}, using the 16 \\texttt{harmful\\_content} pairs at 40--80\\% depth.\n\\item AMS Tier-2 drift: the reference-based verify rule (direction cosine $\\geq 0.8$ and relative separation drift $\\leq 0.2$).\n\\item $B7$: weight-space cosine between the parent's and child's per-layer diff-in-means weight projections, with architecture-mandated null directions projected out.\n\\end{itemize}\nFor each readout, we compute the paired change $\\Delta$ (child minus parent) with a 1000-draw prompt-stratified bootstrap CI. A readout fires a false alarm on a no-op pair if its $\\Delta$ CI excludes zero.\n\n\\subsection{Experiment 2: Causal Intervention Grid}\n\\label{sec:exp2-method}\n\n\\paragraph{Models.}\nWe use three Qwen3-4B variants: Instruct, SafeRL (additional safety reinforcement learning) and an abliterated checkpoint (mlabonne/Qwen3-4B-abliterated).\n\n\\paragraph{Grid design.}\nWe cross six depth bands (B1--B6, each spanning one-sixth of the 36-layer stack) with three sites: P (last prompt token), D$'$ (model's own first 1--8 greedy decode positions, teacher-forced) and E (early response window, positions 5--20). Each cell has four arms:\n\\begin{itemize}\n\\item Arm F: matched-norm projection removing the fitted request-axis direction.\n\\item Arm N6: matched-norm projection removing the benign-side direction.\n\\item Arm R: an orthogonalised random direction with matched norm, averaged over 10--20 draws.\n\\item Arm 0: no intervention (baseline).\n\\end{itemize}\nAn additional positive-control arm (full-residual patching) runs on a two-cell subset.\n\n\\paragraph{Outcomes.}\nFor each cell and arm, we generate 80 new tokens on 48 harmful prompts and 48 benign-borderline prompts and judge refusal, over-refusal and compliance using the same LLM grader as Experiment~1. A cell is \\emph{causal} only if the F (or N6) arm differs from the R arm (not merely from arm 0), to rule out generic disruption. All 18 cells per model are tested jointly with Holm--Bonferroni correction at $\\alpha = 0.05$.\n\n\\paragraph{Decodable-but-inert classification.}\nA cell is classified as ``decodable but inert'' if (a) the direction is linearly decodable from arm-0 activations (AUROC $> 0.70$) and (b) the arm-F (or arm-N6) versus arm-R contrast does not reach significance.\n\n\n\\section{Results}\n\\label{sec:results}\n\n\\subsection{Specificity: False Alarms on Behavioural No-Ops}\n\\label{sec:results-specificity}\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:specificity} reports the false-alarm rate (fraction of no-op pairs where the readout's $\\Delta$ CI excludes zero) and sensitivity (fraction of effective pairs detected) for each readout class.\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{False-alarm rate and sensitivity on 15 behavioural no-ops and 9 effective changes across three families. Activation readouts fire on 0--1 no-ops; logit and weight-space readouts fire on 6--9.}\n\\label{tab:specificity}\n\\begin{tabular}{lccl}\n\\toprule\n\\textbf{Readout} & \\textbf{FA (of 15)} & \\textbf{Sens.\\ (of 9)} & \\textbf{False-alarm pairs} \\\\\n\\midrule\nN6 (benign sep.)       & 0/15 & 5/9 & --- \\\\\nN4 (shape/onset)       & 0/15 & 3/9 & --- \\\\\nN8 (severity $\\rho$)   & 0/15 & 4/8 & --- \\\\\nN9 (decode tok-1)      & 0/15 & 4/8 & --- \\\\\nAMS $\\sigma$ (Tier-1)  & 0/15 & 3/8 & --- \\\\\nN1 (request-axis $d$)  & 1/15 & 5/9 & F3\\_dpo \\\\\nC7 (cross-layer cos)   & 1/15 & 6/9 & F3\\_dpo \\\\\n\\midrule\nBL1\\_easy              & 6/15 & 5/9 & int8wo$\\times$2, sysprompt, wu05$\\times$2, int8bnb \\\\\nBL1\\_truelogit         & 8/15 & 6/9 & +fp16, a05, dpo \\\\\nB7 (weight cosine)     & 9/15 & 7/9 & int8wo$\\times$3, fp16$\\times$3, int8bnb$\\times$2, a05 \\\\\nAMS Tier-2 (drift)     & 0/15 & 0/8 & --- \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\nThe activation readouts (N1, N6, N4, N8, N9, C7, AMS $\\sigma$) fire on at most 1 of 15 no-ops (Wilson 95\\% CI for 1/15: [0.01, 0.30]). The logit baseline BL1\\_easy fires on 6/15 (40\\%; Wilson CI [0.20, 0.64]): int8 weight-only quantisation, system-prompt swaps and head-only unembedding edits all shift the final-layer logit gap without changing judged behaviour. The weight-space cosine B7 is worse still, firing on 9/15 (60\\%). Every dtype cast (fp16, int8wo, int8bnb) moves B7 because the weight matrices change numerically even though behaviour does not.\n\nAmong the baselines, AMS Tier-2 achieves perfect specificity (0/15) but detects zero effective changes (0/8), including five community-abliterated checkpoints. The reference-based verify rule requires the child's direction cosine to exceed 0.8 and its drift to stay below 0.2; abliterated checkpoints violate the cosine threshold but are not flagged because AMS Tier-2 is a \\emph{pass/fail} gate, not a \\emph{change} detector.\n\n\\paragraph{Sensitivity.}\nThe activation readouts detect 3--6 of 9 effective changes. The logit baselines detect 5--6. Neither class reaches the sensitivity of the weight-space cosine (7/9), but B7's sensitivity comes at the cost of a 60\\% false-alarm rate. The trade-off is clear: activation readouts sacrifice some sensitivity for dramatically better specificity.\n\n[FIGURE:fig_specificity]\n\n\n\\subsection{Causal Grid: Decodable but Inert}\n\\label{sec:results-causal}\n\n\\paragraph{No site-local intervention changes judged refusal.}\nAcross the 18-cell grid (6 bands $\\times$ 3 sites), removing the refusal direction F at a single site produces zero causal cells for judged refusal on harmful prompts, in both the instruct and SafeRL models (Table~\\ref{tab:causal_headline}). The same holds for the benign-side direction N6 on harmful compliance, and for the positive control.\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Causal cells surviving Holm correction ($\\alpha = 0.05$) across the 18-cell grid. Refusal on harmful prompts: 0/18 for all arms in all models. Over-refusal on benign-borderline prompts: 1/18 (instruct N6 at P, band B5).}\n\\label{tab:causal_headline}\n\\begin{tabular}{llcccc}\n\\toprule\n\\textbf{Model} & \\textbf{Outcome} & \\textbf{F} & \\textbf{N6} & \\textbf{N6$\\perp$} & \\textbf{POS} \\\\\n\\midrule\nInstruct    & Refused (harm)    & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\\\\nInstruct    & Over-refusal (hb) & 0 & \\textbf{1} & 0 & 0 \\\\\nSafeRL      & Refused (harm)    & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\\\\nSafeRL      & Over-refusal (hb) & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\\\\nAbliterated & Refused (harm)    & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\\\\nAbliterated & Over-refusal (hb) & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\paragraph{Token-1 moves but judged refusal does not.}\nRemoving F at the prompt site in bands B4--B6 shifts the first-token refusal-onset log-mass by $-2.9$ nats in the instruct model. A keyword-based refusal proxy drops from 0.79 to 0.15, which would appear as a successful jailbreak under keyword-matching evaluation. However, the LLM-judged refusal rate does not change: the model replaces its canonical refusal phrasing (e.g., ``I'm unable to help with that'') with alternative formulations (e.g., ``Creating malware is illegal and I cannot assist''). SafeRL uses ``It's important to clarify'' as its refusal template, which the keyword proxy does not recognise at all ($\\kappa = 0$ between keyword and judge labels for SafeRL).\n\n\\paragraph{Decodable but inert.}\nTable~\\ref{tab:decodable_inert} reports the count of cells classified as decodable but inert: the direction is linearly decodable from arm-0 activations but removing it does not change judged behaviour.\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Decodable-but-inert cells. The refusal direction F is decodable at the prompt site in every cell where the model refuses, yet removing it never changes judged refusal.}\n\\label{tab:decodable_inert}\n\\begin{tabular}{lcc}\n\\toprule\n\\textbf{Model} & \\textbf{F on refused\\_harm} & \\textbf{N6 on over-refusal} \\\\\n\\midrule\nInstruct    & 12/12 & 11/12 \\\\\nSafeRL      & 12/12 & 12/12 \\\\\nAbliterated &  6/6  &  6/6  \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\paragraph{Over-refusal is the causal lever.}\nThe single cell that survives Holm correction is N6 at site P, band B5, for over-refusal on benign-borderline prompts in the instruct model. Over-refusal drops by 0.12--0.19 at bands B4--B5 before correction. SafeRL shows no causal over-refusal cells: global removal of F at band B4 drops instruct refusal to 0.67, but SafeRL's difference-in-differences is $+0.23$, consistent with its additional safety reinforcement learning providing deeper redundancy.\n\n\\paragraph{Abliterated checkpoint.}\nThe abliterated model's refusal direction has cosine similarity $\\sim$0.3 with the instruct direction from band B4 onward, compared to $\\sim$0.9 at bands B1--B3. Removing the abliterated model's own fitted F direction at the prompt site \\emph{raises} refusal-onset log-mass, the opposite of the instruct pattern. The abliteration procedure rotates the representation rather than erasing it, consistent with Galeone et al.'s finding that detection and control are dissociated \\cite{Galeone2026}.\n\n[FIGURE:fig_causal_grid]\n\n\n\\subsection{Commissioned Qwen3-4B Comparison}\n\\label{sec:results-qwen}\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:qwen_arms} reports the five Qwen3-4B variants on the readouts from both experiments.\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\caption{Qwen3-4B variants. BL1 ranks SafeRL below Instruct (3.07 vs 4.99) despite comparable refusal behaviour. N1 and N6 rank them correctly. The abliterated checkpoint's N1 drops while N6 (benign-side) barely moves.}\n\\label{tab:qwen_arms}\n\\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}\n\\toprule\n\\textbf{Variant} & \\textbf{HC} & \\textbf{OR} & $\\bm{N1}$ & $\\bm{N6}$ & \\textbf{BL1} & \\textbf{AMS $\\sigma$} \\\\\n\\midrule\nBase          & 0.02 & 0.00 & 0.54  & 0.30  & 0.32  & 1.21 \\\\\nInstruct      & 0.00 & 0.11 & 2.45  & 1.87  & 4.99  & 5.73 \\\\\nSafeRL        & 0.00 & 0.00 & 2.34  & 2.12  & 3.07  & 6.41 \\\\\nAbliterated   & 0.73 & 0.00 & 0.71  & 1.79  & 1.76  & 2.08 \\\\\nSTaR          & NA   & NA   & 0.59  & 0.45  & 0.63  & 1.89 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\nTwo patterns emerge. First, BL1 ranks SafeRL below Instruct (3.07 vs 4.99) despite SafeRL having zero harmful compliance and zero over-refusal, while Instruct has 11\\% over-refusal. N1 and AMS $\\sigma$ rank SafeRL and Instruct comparably (2.34 vs 2.45; 6.41 vs 5.73). Second, the abliterated checkpoint's N6 (benign-side separability, 1.79) barely drops from Instruct's value (1.87), while N1 drops sharply (0.71 vs 2.45). The model retains the representation that distinguishes safe from borderline content even after the execution-side refusal direction is removed, consistent with the recognition-execution dissociation reported by Orgad et al.\\ \\cite{Orgad2026}.\n\n\n\\section{Discussion}\n\\label{sec:discussion}\n\n\\subsection{Why Logit Baselines Fail the Specificity Test}\n\nThe final-layer logit gap measures the difference between the probability of the top refusal token and the top compliance token at the last prompt position. Any perturbation that shifts these probabilities---even by a small amount that does not change the greedy decode---produces a nonzero $\\Delta$BL1. Quantisation and dtype casts change the numerical precision of the logit computation, system-prompt swaps change the input distribution, and head-only unembedding edits change the projection matrix. All of these move BL1 without moving behaviour because BL1 operates at the decision boundary while behaviour depends on the argmax.\n\nActivation readouts, by contrast, measure the geometry of the representation space at mid-depth layers, which is more stable under these perturbations. The diff-in-means direction at layer 14 of Qwen3-0.6B is bitwise identical between the bf16 reference and the fp16 cast (the activations are computed in bf16 regardless of storage precision), and the int8 weight-only round-trip changes activations by less than $10^{-3}$ in norm.\n\n\\subsection{Decodable but Inert: Implications for Safety Monitoring}\n\nThe finding that the refusal direction is decodable at the prompt site but removing it does not change judged refusal has two implications. First, keyword-based refusal detection is unreliable. The keyword proxy reports a 64-percentage-point drop in refusal under site-local F removal, but this reflects a change in phrasing, not in policy. An evaluation that counts ``I cannot'' as refusal and ``This is illegal and I cannot assist'' as compliance will overestimate the effectiveness of interventions. Second, the model's refusal policy is implemented redundantly. Even after the dominant linear direction is removed at one site, the model recovers its refusal through alternative representations or later layers. Global removal of F at all positions and all layers does reduce judged refusal (instruct drops to 0.67), confirming that the direction carries causal information in aggregate, but no single site is sufficient.\n\nThis finding extends Galeone et al.'s detection-control dissociation \\cite{Galeone2026} from the cross-model setting (where different models show different steerability) to the within-model setting (where different sites within the same model show different causal strength).\n\n\\subsection{Limitations}\n\\label{sec:limitations}\n\n\\textbf{Scale.} The specificity audit uses three families at 0.6--1.7B parameters. Larger models may have different false-alarm profiles, and the 15 no-ops, while spanning a range of deployment-relevant modifications, do not cover every possible perturbation.\n\n\\textbf{Sensitivity gap.} The activation readouts detect 3--6 of 9 effective changes compared to 5--6 for BL1. Whether this gap closes at larger panel sizes is an open question that the pre-registered confirmation panel (at least 30 new checkpoints from at least 8 new families) is designed to answer.\n\n\\textbf{Single architecture for the causal grid.} The causal experiment uses only Qwen3-4B variants. The decodable-but-inert finding may not hold for architectures with different attention patterns or layer counts.\n\n\\textbf{Judge limitations.} All behavioural outcomes depend on an LLM judge. The judge achieves high agreement with human labels on a calibration set, but systematic biases (e.g., toward labelling longer responses as compliant) cannot be ruled out.\n\n\\textbf{No surviving candidate.} No readout passes the full pre-registered selection rule, because the required gap of 1.0 null-SD below BL1's median no-op displacement is unattainable: the activation readouts' median displacement is already near zero, and BL1's is only moderately above zero. The pre-registered bar was set before the magnitude of BL1's false-alarm rate was known.\n\n\n\\section{Conclusion}\n\\label{sec:conclusion}\n\nWe audited activation-based safety readouts for two properties that a replacement for behavioural benchmarks must have: specificity (no false alarms on no-ops) and causal relevance (the direction matters for behaviour, not just for a probe). Activation readouts at mid-layer depth pass the specificity test with at most 1/15 false alarms, while the final-layer logit gap fails it with 6--8/15. The causal grid reveals that the refusal direction is decodable at every prompt-site cell but removing it changes the first token without changing judged refusal---a dissociation between the keyword proxy and actual safety behaviour that calls for judge-based evaluation in future intervention studies. The single causal lever is over-refusal under the benign-side direction, and SafeRL provides deeper redundancy than standard instruction tuning. These findings establish the false-alarm audit as a necessary validation step for any activation-based safety metric and identify the decodable-but-inert phenomenon as a constraint on site-local causal claims.\n\n\\bibliography{references}\n\\bibliographystyle{plainnat}\n", "numLines": 256, "startLine": 1, "totalLines": 256}}

The decodable-but-inert finding may not hold for architectures with different attention patterns or layer counts.\n\n\\textbf{Judge limitations.} All behavioural outcomes depend on an LLM judge. The judge achieves high agreement with human labels on a calibration set, but systematic biases (e.g., toward labelling longer responses as compliant) cannot be ruled out.\n\n\\textbf{No surviving candidate.} No readout passes the full pre-registered selection rule, because the required gap of 1.0 null-SD below BL1's median no-op displacement is unattainable: the activation readouts' median displacement is already near zero, and BL1's is only moderately above zero. The pre-registered bar was set before the magnitude of BL1's false-alarm rate was known.\n\n\n\\section{Conclusion}\n\\label{sec:conclusion}\n\nWe audited activation-based safety readouts for two properties that a replacement for behavioural benchmarks must have: specificity (no false alarms on no-ops) and causal relevance (the direction matters for behaviour, not just for a probe). Activation readouts at mid-layer depth pass the specificity test with at most 1/15 false alarms, while the final-layer logit gap fails it with 6--8/15. The causal grid reveals that the refusal direction is decodable at every prompt-site cell but removing it changes the first token without changing judged refusal---a dissociation between the keyword proxy and actual safety behaviour that calls for judge-based evaluation in future intervention studies. The single causal lever is over-refusal under the benign-side direction, and SafeRL provides deeper redundancy than standard instruction tuning. These findings establish the false-alarm audit as a necessary validation step for any activation-based safety metric and identify the decodable-but-inert phenomenon as a constraint on site-local causal claims.\n\n\\bibliography{references}\n\\bibliographystyle{plainnat}\n", "numLines": 259, "startLine": 1, "totalLines": 259}}

The proliferation of post-hoc modifications to released checkpoints, in particular abliteration, a rank-one weight edit that removes a model's refusal direction \\\\cite{Arditi2024}, makes repeated evaluation expensive and raises the question of whether safety-relevant information can be read directly from a model's internal representations.\\n\\nRecent work has shown that safety-relevant information is linearly decodable from mid-layer activations. The technique has been applied to produce ``uncensored'' checkpoints for Qwen, LLaMA, Phi, SmolLM, and Granite families, many of which are publicly available on Hugging Face. Public abliteration toolkits already compute pairwise cosine similarities and cumulative angular drift across layers \\\\cite{Arditi2024}.\\n\\n\\n\\\\section{Method}\\n\\\\label{sec:method}\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Models and Checkpoints}\\n\\\\label{sec:models}\\n\\nLane~A uses 25 checkpoints spanning five families: Qwen3 (0.6B, 1.7B, 4B), Qwen2.5 (1.5B), SmolLM3 (3B), SmolLM2 (1.7B), Phi-4-mini, Granite-3.2 (2B), TinyLlama (1.1B), OLMo-2 (1B), and StableLM-2 (1.6B). For the Lane~B lesion study, we use 384 harmful and 384 benign items drawn from AdvBench and paired benign corpora, split into 128 EASY prompts (fit set) and 256 HARD prompts (held-out evaluation set), with leave-one-family-out cross-validation across harm categories.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Readouts and Notation}\\n\\\\label{sec:notation}\\n\\nTable~\\\\ref{tab:notation} defines all readouts and notation used in the paper.\\n\\n\\\\begin{table}[t]\\n\\\\centering\\n\\\\small\\n\\\\caption{Notation and readout definitions.}\\n\\\\label{tab:notation}\\n\\\\begin{tabular}{lp{9cm}}\\n\\\\toprule\\n\\\\textbf{Symbol} & \\\\textbf{Definition} \\\\\\\\\\n\\\\midrule\\n$d$ (held-out) & Request-axis Cohen's $d$: the diff-in-means axis is fit on EASY prompts at the best layer, then scored on HARD prompts. Measures prompt-site separability of harmful vs.\\\\ benign requests. \\\\\\\\\\n$R$ (TPR@$k$\\\\%FPR) & Recognition: true positive rate of a logistic probe at $k$\\\\% false positive rate, classifying harmful vs.\\\\ benign requests from prompt-site activations. Fit on a random half, scored on the other. \\\\\\\\\\nPeak drive & Maximum across layers of the logit-lens projection onto the refusal token direction, measured at the last prompt token. \\\\\\\\\\nBL1 & Final-layer logit gap: the logit difference between the top refusal token and the top compliance token at the last prompt position in the final layer. \\\\\\\\\\nHC & Harmful compliance rate: fraction of harmful prompts answered substantively. \\\\\\\\\\nOR & Over-refusal rate: fraction of benign prompts incorrectly refused. \\\\\\\\\\nOnset depth & Earliest layer (as a fraction of total depth) at which a diff-in-means probe achieves $d > 1$ on HARD prompts. \\\\\\\\\\n$B3$ & Direction self-consistency: Fisher-transformed mean cosine similarity of per-layer diff-in-means directions across consecutive layers. \\\\\\\\\\n$\\\\alpha$ & Abliteration dose in the rank-one lesion $W \\\\leftarrow W - \\\\alpha \\\\cdot u(u^\\\\top W)$; $\\\\alpha = 0$ is intact, $\\\\alpha = 1$ is full abliteration. \\\\\\\\\\nPROMPT site & Activations at the last prompt token. \\\\\\\\\\nEARLY site & Activations at response tokens 5--20 (teacher-forced harmful continuation). \\\\\\\\\\nLATE site & Activations at response tokens 40--55. \\\\\\\\\\n\\\\bottomrule\\n\\\\end{tabular}\\n\\\\end{table}\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Lane~A: Checkpoint Panel}\\n\\\\label{sec:lane-a}\\n\\nFor each of the 25 checkpoints, we extract residual-stream activations at every layer for the prompt tokens and, where the model produces or is fed a harmful continuation, at the response tokens. We compute six activation readouts: held-out $d$, $R$ at TPR@5\\\\%FPR, peak refusal drive, onset depth, $k$-prompt AUROC at $k \\\\in \\\\{4, 8, 16\\\\}$, and direction self-consistency $B3$. Each is reported beside the logit baseline BL1. We additionally compute the accumulator test: the norm-controlled gap along a direction frozen at the shallowest band layer (layer 13 for Qwen3-4B), tracked forward through depth, and compare it to the gap along a per-layer refit direction.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Lane~B: Dose-Graded Rank-One Lesion}\\n\\\\label{sec:lane-b}\\n\\nWe fit the abliteration direction $u$ from 128 AdvBench prompts and apply the rank-one edit at layers 13--21 (the band identified by the abliteration recipe) at five dose levels. At each dose, we record activations at three sites---PROMPT, EARLY, and LATE---and fit a logistic probe (trained at $\\\\alpha = 0$) to classify harmful vs.\\\\ benign items. The probe's TPR at 1\\\\%FPR and 5\\\\%FPR across dose levels measures how the lesion affects separability at each site. Four lineages are constructed: L1 (Instruct), L2 (Instruct, different random seed for the direction), L3 (SafeRL), and L4 (STaR, a non-safety fine-tune that does not refuse).\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Lane~C: Cross-Family Validation}\\n\\\\label{sec:lane-c}\\n\\nLane~C computes each activation readout on the 10 held-out checkpoints and correlates them with harmful compliance. We report Spearman $\\\\rho$ with HC, the paired difference from BL1's $\\\\rho$, and family-bootstrap confidence intervals that resample at the family level to account for within-family dependence. A readout is counted as exceeding BL1 only if the paired $\\\\rho$ difference has a 95\\\\% CI that excludes zero.\\n\\n\\n\\\\section{Results}\\n\\\\label{sec:results}\\n\\n\\\\subsection{What Safety Tuning and Abliteration Move}\\n\\\\label{sec:results-what-moves}\\n\\nTable~\\\\ref{tab:main} shows the five Qwen3-4B variants on all readouts. Safety training (Base $\\\\to$ Instruct) raises every readout: held-out $d$ rises from 0.54 to 2.45, recognition TPR@5\\\\%FPR rises from 0.475 to 0.875 (paired-bootstrap 90\\\\% CI on the delta: [0.137, 0.762]), peak refusal drive rises from 1.57 to 4.92, and BL1 rises from 0.32 to 4.99. The non-safety fine-tune (STaR) matches Base only on held-out $d$: the difference is 0.046 (TOST-equivalent at $\\\\pm 0.5$). On other readouts, STaR moves partway toward Instruct, covering 33\\\\% of the Base-to-Instruct distance on peak drive and 46\\\\% on BL1, indicating that part of the refusal-drive signal reflects generic chat fine-tuning rather than safety training alone.\\n\\n\\\\begin{table}[t]\\n\\\\centering\\n\\\\small\\n\\\\caption{Readouts for five Qwen3-4B variants. Safety training moves all readouts. Abliteration drops $d$ and drive while recognition $R$ barely moves. STaR matches Base only on $d$.}\\n\\\\label{tab:main}\\n\\\\begin{tabular}{lccccccc}\\n\\\\toprule\\n\\\\textbf{Checkpoint} & \\\\textbf{HC} & $\\\\bm{d}$ & $\\\\bm{R}$ & \\\\textbf{Drive} & \\\\textbf{BL1} & \\\\textbf{Onset} & $\\\\bm{B3}$ \\\\\\\\\\n\\\\midrule\\nBase          & 0.022 & 0.54  & 0.475 & 1.57  & 0.32  & 0.92 & 2.58  \\\\\\\\\\nInstruct      & 0.000 & 2.45  & 0.875 & 4.92  & 4.99  & 0.53 & 28.14 \\\\\\\\\\nSafeRL        & 0.000 & 2.34  & 0.850 & 8.78  & 3.07  & 0.53 & 33.15 \\\\\\\\\\nSTaR          & NA    & 0.59  & 0.713 & 2.57  & 0.63  & 0.64 & 0.27  \\\\\\\\\\nAbliterated   & 0.733 & 0.71  & 0.838 & 1.92  & 1.76  & 0.53 & 0.54  \\\\\\\\\\n\\\\midrule\\nRandInit      & NA    & 0.20  & 0.075 & 0.07  & 0.02  & 0.04 & 4.85  \\\\\\\\\\n\\\\bottomrule\\n\\\\end{tabular}\\n\\\\end{table}\\n\\nAbliteration produces the opposite pattern from safety training: the held-out request-axis $d$ drops from 2.45 (Instruct) to 0.71 ($\\\\Delta = -1.73$, 95\\\\% CI $[-2.35, -1.19]$), and peak drive drops from 4.92 to 1.92 (near the Base value of 1.57). Recognition, measured by the nested HARD-refit probe, barely moves: $\\\\Delta R = -0.037$ (90\\\\% CI $[-0.150, 0.125]$, inconclusive due to power). This dissociation (separability collapses while the probe still classifies) replicates across six effective parent--child pairs from four families: all six show $d$ drops with 95\\\\% CIs below zero, while the Granite null-edit control (same model re-downloaded) shows $\\\\Delta d = 0.09$ (CI includes zero). The dissociation also holds on two new abliterated pairs in the held-out panel (Section~\\\\ref{sec:results-heldout}).\\n\\nThe claim ``execution, not recognition'' therefore describes only what abliteration removes, not what safety training adds. Safety training raises both recognition and the refusal drive simultaneously.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{The Harm Direction Is Layer-Specific}\\n\\\\label{sec:results-depth}\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig_accumulator]\\n\\nA previous iteration of this work reported that the class gap along a fitted direction grows approximately 138-fold from layer 13 to the fitting layer, suggesting an accumulator mechanism. The iter-3 evaluation runs the decisive control: the same gap measured along a direction frozen at layer 13, tracked forward through depth.\\n\\nThe fixed-axis gap does not grow. In every arm (Base, Instruct, SafeRL, STaR, and Abliterated), the norm-controlled gap along the layer-13 axis decays with depth. The Spearman correlation between gap magnitude and layer index is strongly negative: $-0.99$ (Base), $-0.82$ (Instruct), $-0.87$ (SafeRL), $-0.97$ (STaR), $-0.88$ (Abliterated). The fixed-axis peak-to-start ratio is 1.00 in all arms: the gap never exceeds its initial value.\\n\\nSeparation is maintained only when the diff-in-means axis is refit at each layer. The per-layer refit ratio (gap at layer $\\\\ell$ along $u_\\\\ell$ divided by gap at layer 13 along $u_{13}$) ranges from 1.41 (Abliterated) to 2.09 (SafeRL). The HARD-scored variant of this ratio reaches 19.7 for Instruct, reflecting the emergence of a distinct deep-layer direction that separates harmful from benign requests on out-of-distribution prompts.\\n\\nThe harm direction is therefore layer-specific: shallow and deep representations encode harmfulness along different coordinates, and a single accumulated direction does not capture the trajectory. This pattern holds identically in all four Lane~B lineages across all five dose levels and all three activation sites.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Response-Site Fragility Under Lesion}\\n\\\\label{sec:results-site}\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig_site]\\n\\nTable~\\\\ref{tab:site} reports the change in TPR@1\\\\%FPR from $\\\\alpha = 0$ (intact) to $\\\\alpha = 1$ (full lesion) for each lineage at each of the three sites. At the PROMPT site, the change is small and includes zero in every lineage: L1 $-0.042$ [$-0.094$, $0.021$], L2 $-0.010$ [$-0.177$, $0.073$], L3 $+0.031$ [$-0.271$, $0.250$], L4 $-0.094$ [$-0.146$, $0.010$]. At the EARLY response site, changes are also small and include zero. At the LATE response site, every lineage shows a drop: L1 $-0.083$, L2 $-0.185$, L3 $-0.138$, L4 $-0.169$.\\n\\n\\\\begin{table}[t]\\n\\\\centering\\n\\\\small\\n\\\\caption{Change in TPR@1\\\\%FPR from $\\\\alpha=0$ to $\\\\alpha=1$, per lineage and site. LATE-site drops are comparable in the non-safety lineage L4, so the effect is not safety-specific.}\\n\\\\label{tab:site}\\n\\\\begin{tabular}{lcccc}\\n\\\\toprule\\n\\\\textbf{Site} & \\\\textbf{L1 (Instruct)} & \\\\textbf{L2 (Instruct)} & \\\\textbf{L3 (SafeRL)} & \\\\textbf{L4 (STaR)} \\\\\\\\\\n\\\\midrule\\nPROMPT & $-0.042$ & $-0.010$ & $+0.031$ & $-0.094$ \\\\\\\\\\nEARLY  & $-0.039$ & $+0.031$ & $+0.049$ & $-0.039$ \\\\\\\\\\nLATE   & $-0.083$ & $-0.185$ & $-0.138$ & $-0.169$ \\\\\\\\\\n\\\\bottomrule\\n\\\\end{tabular}\\n\\\\end{table}\\n\\nThe critical comparison is L4, the non-safety fine-tune. L4 does not refuse harmful prompts, so any late-site drop under the lesion cannot be interpreted as loss of a safety-execution mechanism. L4's LATE-site drop ($-0.169$) is comparable to or larger than L1's ($-0.083$). The safety-minus-L4 contrasts all have 95\\\\% CIs that include zero: L1$-$L4 = $-0.086$ [$-0.185$, $0.096$]; L2$-$L4 = $+0.016$ [$-0.149$, $0.240$]; L3$-$L4 = $-0.031$ [$-0.164$, $0.208$]. The late-response drop therefore reads as generic disruption of the response-site representation under a rank-one edit, not as loss of a safety-specific execution signal.\\n\\nSub-threshold doses ($\\\\alpha \\\\leq 0.50$) produce effects that are TOST-equivalent to zero in every lineage at every site. Only the full lesion ($\\\\alpha = 1.0$) yields significant drops at the LATE site.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Held-Out Panel and Cross-Family Transfer}\\n\\\\label{sec:results-heldout}\\n\\n[FIGURE:fig_heldout]\\n\\nTable~\\\\ref{tab:heldout} reports Spearman correlations with harmful compliance for the six activation readouts and BL1 on the 10-checkpoint held-out panel.\\n\\n\\\\begin{table}[t]\\n\\\\centering\\n\\\\small\\n\\\\caption{Spearman $\\\\rho$ with harmful compliance on the 10-checkpoint held-out panel. $B3$ achieves the strongest correlation but the paired delta from BL1 does not exclude zero at family-bootstrap 95\\\\% CI.}\\n\\\\label{tab:heldout}\\n\\\\begin{tabular}{lcccc}\\n\\\\toprule\\n\\\\textbf{Readout} & $\\\\bm{\\\\rho}$ & \\\\textbf{Family 95\\\\% CI} & \\\\textbf{$\\\\Delta$ vs BL1} & \\\\textbf{Partial $\\\\rho$|BL1} \\\\\\\\\\n\\\\midrule\\n$B3$ (self-consistency) & $-0.890$ & $[-0.951, -0.569]$ & $-0.270$ & $-0.816$ \\\\\\\\\\n$C13$ (peak $d$)        & $-0.656$ & $[-0.975, 0.200]$  & $-0.037$ & $-0.433$ \\\\\\\\\\nBL1                     & $-0.620$ & $[-0.735, 0.200]$  & ---      & --- \\\\\\\\\\nBL1\\\\_hard               & $-0.534$ & $[-0.705, 0.413]$  & ---      & --- \\\\\\\\\\n\\\\bottomrule\\n\\\\end{tabular}\\n\\\\end{table}\\n\\nDirection self-consistency ($B3$) achieves $\\\\rho = -0.890$ with HC, substantially stronger than BL1's $\\\\rho = -0.620$. However, the paired delta of $-0.270$ has a family-bootstrap 95\\\\% CI that, at $n = 10$ with four families, does not exclude zero. The partial correlation of $B3$ with HC given BL1 is $-0.816$, indicating that $B3$ captures variance in harmful compliance that BL1 does not, but the sample is too small to confirm this at the cross-family level. Two new abliterated pairs in the held-out panel replicate the within-family dissociation: held-out $d$ drops in both (CIs below zero), consistent with the six Lane~A pairs.\\n\\nAcross the 25-checkpoint Lane~A panel, every activation readout correlates with BL1 at $\\\\rho > 0.71$ (Table~\\\\ref{tab:bl1corr}). The partial Spearman correlation with HC after controlling for BL1 is $-0.464$ for held-out $d$, $-0.468$ for $B3$, $-0.327$ for peak drive, and $+0.017$ for recognition $R$. Recognition therefore carries no information beyond the logit baseline at the panel level. Held-out $d$ and $B3$ retain partial correlations of moderate magnitude, but these were not pre-registered and must be interpreted with caution given the small family count.\\n\\n\\\\begin{table}[t]\\n\\\\centering\\n\\\\small\\n\\\\caption{Correlation of each activation readout with BL1 across the 25-checkpoint panel. All activation readouts track BL1 closely.}\\n\\\\label{tab:bl1corr}\\n\\\\begin{tabular}{lcc}\\n\\\\toprule\\n\\\\textbf{Readout} & $\\\\bm{\\\\rho}$ \\\\textbf{with BL1} & \\\\textbf{Partial $\\\\rho$ with HC $|$ BL1} \\\\\\\\\\n\\\\midrule\\nHeld-out $d$  & 0.767 & $-0.464$ \\\\\\\\\\n$R$ TPR@5\\\\%   & 0.791 & $+0.017$ \\\\\\\\\\nPeak drive    & 0.784 & $-0.327$ \\\\\\\\\\n$B3$          & 0.715 & $-0.468$ \\\\\\\\\\n$k_{16}$ AUROC & 0.746 & $-0.390$ \\\\\\\\\\n\\\\bottomrule\\n\\\\end{tabular}\\n\\\\end{table}\\n\\n\\n\\\\section{Discussion}\\n\\\\label{sec:discussion}\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Layer-Specific Harm Directions}\\n\\nThe layer-specific harm direction has implications for both the mechanistic understanding of safety and for practical readout design. The decay of the fixed-axis gap with depth means that a probe fitted at one layer cannot be applied at another without re-estimation. The growth seen in earlier reports (the ``138-fold'' increase along the fitting-layer axis) was an artefact of measuring each layer's representation on a direction optimised for the final layer: any direction fitted at one layer is most discriminative there. The informative quantity is the per-layer refit ratio, which shows modest growth (1.4--2.1$\\\\times$) and reflects the emergence of a new harm-relevant direction at each depth, not accumulation along a single coordinate.\\n\\nThis finding is consistent with Galeone et al.'s report that weight cosines between layer-wise directions are low and do not predict steerability \\\\cite{Galeone2026}, and with the observation in public abliteration toolkits that consecutive-layer cosines can be as low as 0.016 in deep layers.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Why No Activation Metric Beats the Logit Gap}\\n\\nFor the Instruct model, the peak refusal-drive layer is the final layer: peak drive equals BL1 (4.92). Both readouts drop 6/6 in effective abliterated pairs, and both also drop on the Granite null-edit control (a re-download of the same model with no behavioural change, where $\\\\Delta$BL1 $= -4.83$ and $\\\\Delta$peak\\\\_drive $= -2.49$ but $\\\\Delta d = 0.09$). The held-out request-axis $d$ is the one readout that does not move on the null edit, making it the most specific activation readout---but it does not separate safety-tuned from abliterated at cross-family scale with $n = 10$.\\n\\nThe core difficulty is that at the panel sizes available (25 checkpoints, 10 held-out, 4--5 families), the activation readouts are too correlated with the logit gap ($\\\\rho > 0.71$) to demonstrate independent predictive value. AMS achieves leave-one-out threshold accuracy of 71\\\\% on 14 checkpoints from four families \\\\cite{Yang2026}, and its $\\\\sigma$ statistic is the current external bar for activation-based safety readouts. Our panel does not include AMS's checkpoints, so a direct head-to-head comparison is not available, but the logit baseline already matches or exceeds every activation readout we tested. A larger, more diverse panel would be needed to resolve whether the partial correlations of $B3$ and held-out $d$ reflect genuine additional information or sampling noise at small $n$.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Limitations}\\n\\\\label{sec:limitations}\\n\\n\\\\textbf{Architecture scope.} All five Lane~A Qwen3-4B variants share one architecture. The 10 held-out checkpoints span four additional families but at $n = 10$ with four families, cross-family conclusions have wide confidence intervals.\\n\\n\\\\textbf{Prompt-only for $d$.} The request-axis Cohen's $d$ is computed at the prompt site only. A response-site variant was not tested, so we cannot determine whether it would capture information that the prompt-site version misses.\\n\\n\\\\textbf{No causal intervention at response site.} The Lane~B lesion study measures the effect of the rank-one edit on response-site representations, but does not perform a targeted causal intervention (e.g., activation patching) at the response site to confirm that the representations there are used by downstream computation.\\n\\n\\\\textbf{Teacher-forced continuations.} Response-site activations in Lane~B come from teacher-forced harmful completions, not from the model's own generations. The activations may differ from those produced during free generation, especially for models that would refuse.\\n\\n\\\\textbf{Saturation.} Probe AUROC is 1.00 at every layer and dose level, so it cannot detect degradation. We report TPR at low FPR as a de-saturated alternative, but with $n = 384$ negatives, TPR@1\\\\%FPR is set by approximately 4 items and has resolution 0.0026.\\n\\n\\\\textbf{Gates.} Of 68 pre-registered quality gates, 43 pass and 24 fail. G1 (split-half AUROC stability within 0.02) and G5 (placebo TOST equivalence) fail in all arms. G6 (subtraction licensing) holds only in non-safety arms. These failures do not invalidate the main results but limit the precision of secondary analyses.\\n\\n\\\\textbf{The commissioned metric.} The original request asked for an activation-based metric that could evaluate any model's safety from zero to a few prompts. This metric is not delivered: no activation readout beats the logit baseline at cross-family scale. The $k$-prompt AUROC scan has smallest\\\\_$k$\\\\_pass = null for all candidates. We report this negative result as the honest outcome of the study.\\n\\n\\n\\\\section{Conclusion}\\n\\\\label{sec:conclusion}\\n\\nWe profiled safety-relevant representations across 25 checkpoints from five model families, using three complementary measurement lanes. Four findings emerged. First, safety training raises both prompt-site recognition and refusal drive; abliteration dissociates them, dropping the held-out request-axis $d$ from 2.45 to 0.71 while recognition barely changes. This dissociation replicates across six parent--child pairs. Second, the harm direction is layer-specific: the gap along a frozen shallow-layer axis decays with depth in all five Qwen3-4B variants. Third, the late-response-site fragility under rank-one lesion is not safety-specific: the non-safety fine-tune shows a comparable drop, and no safety-minus-control contrast excludes zero. Fourth, on a 10-checkpoint held-out panel, direction self-consistency ($B3$, $\\\\rho = -0.89$) correlates most strongly with harmful compliance, but the paired margin over the logit baseline does not reach significance at the family level.\\n\\nThe practical implication is that, at current panel sizes, the final-layer logit gap remains the bar that activation-based safety readouts must beat. The mechanistic implication is that safety information is not stored in a single accumulated coordinate but is rewritten at each depth into a new direction, and that response-site effects of abliteration are generic rather than safety-specific. Both findings constrain how future activation-based safety metrics should be designed: they should account for layer-specific rotation and should be validated against the logit baseline on panels large enough to resolve partial correlations at the family level.\\n\",\n \"figures\": [\n  {\n   \"id\": \"fig_overview\",\n   \"title\": \"Three-Lane Study Design\",\n   \"caption\": \"Overview of the three-lane study. Y-axis (categorical, top to bottom): 'B3 (self-consistency)', 'C13 (peak d)', 'BL1 (logit gap)', 'BL1_hard'. X-axis: 'Spearman rho with harmful compliance' from -1.0 to 0.5. A vertical dashed line at x=0. Bar values with horizontal error bars (family-bootstrap 95% CI): B3: rho=-0.890, CI=[-0.951, -0.569], bar coloured dark green. The logit baselines detect 5--6. Neither class reaches the sensitivity of the weight-space cosine (7/9), but B7's sensitivity comes at the cost of a 60\\% false-alarm rate. The abliterated checkpoint's N1 drops while N6 (benign-side) barely moves.}\n\\label{tab:qwen_arms}\n\\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}\n\\toprule\n\\textbf{Variant} & \\textbf{HC} & \\textbf{OR} & $\\bm{N1}$ & $\\bm{N6}$ & \\textbf{BL1} & \\textbf{AMS $\\sigma$} \\\\\n\\midrule\nBase          & 0.02 & 0.00 & 0.54  & 0.30  & 0.32  & 1.21 \\\\\nInstruct      & 0.00 & 0.11 & 2.45  & 1.87  & 4.99  & 5.73 \\\\\nSafeRL        & 0.00 & 0.00 & 2.34  & 2.12  & 3.07  & 6.41 \\\\\nAbliterated   & 0.73 & 0.00 & 0.71  & 1.79  & 1.76  & 2.08 \\\\\nSTaR          & NA   & NA   & 0.59  & 0.45  & 0.63  & 1.89 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\nTwo patterns emerge.
